'''''Leucospermum cuneiforme''''' is an upright evergreen shrub with many pustules growing on the lower branches, wedge-shaped leaves, and oval, initially yellow flower heads that later turn orange, with long styles sticking far beyond the perianths, jointly giving the impression of a pincushion. It is called '''wart-stemmed pincushion''' in English and '''{{Lang|af|luisiesbos}}''' (lice-bush) in [[Afrikaans]]. The species is common in the southern mountains of South Africa.<ref name=IDENT>{{cite web|website= Protea Atlas Project|title= Identifying Pincushions|url= https://www.proteaatlas.org.za/pincushid.htm}}</ref><ref name=SANBI>{{cite web|website= SANBI|title= Leucospermum cuneiforme (Burm.f.) Rourke|url= http://pza.sanbi.org/leucospermum-cuneiforme}}</ref>

== Description ==
''Leucospermum cuneiforme'' is an upright, [[evergreen]] shrub, often of only ½–1 m (1½–3 ft) high, that has branches that originate from a woody rootstock in the ground, and if protected against fire will develop a main stem and grows up to {{convert|3|m|ft|abbr=on}} high. The stem and lower branches are covered in pustules, a unique feature for this species. The upright flowering branches are {{convert|3–7|mm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter and appear to be grey due to soft, crinkly hairs. The leaves are hairless, narrow to broadly wedge-shaped 4½–11 cm (1.8–4.4 in) long and {{convert|0.6–3|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide, with three to ten teeth with bony tips near the far end of the leaf.<ref name=Rourke /><ref name=JSTOR>{{cite web|website= JSTOR Global Plants|title= Compilation Leucospermum zeyheri|url= https://plants.jstor.org/compilation/Leucospermum.zeyheri}}</ref>

The flower heads sitting usually solitary or grouped with two or three near the end of the branches, are egg-shaped, {{convert|5–9|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter each on a [[Peduncle (botany)|stalk]] of up to 1½ cm (0.6 in) long. The [[Receptacle (botany)|common base]] of the flowers within the same head is cylindric with a blunt tip, 2½–4½ cm (1.0–1.8 in) long and {{convert|6|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide. The [[Bract#Involucral bracts|bracts]] that subtend the flower head are broadly oval with a pointy tip, about {{convert|0.8-1.0|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|6|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide, closely overlapping, rubbery in consistency, grey due to the dense soft hair. The [[Bract#Bracteole|bracts that subtend the individual flower]] are oval with a pointy tip,  {{convert|1.0–1.2|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and about {{convert|7|mm|in|abbr=on}} wide, rubbery in consistency, embracing the foot of the perianth, densely woolly at the base, less dense nearer the tip and with a dense row of hairs around the fringes. The [[perianth]] is 2½–4 cm (1.0–1.6 in) long, curved towards the center of the flower head in bud. It is initially yellow, but later changes to orange, although the colour differs across the range. Its base is fused into a tube of {{convert|6–10|mm|in|abbr=on}} long, a bit laterally compressed, smooth near the base and with a minutely powdery covering near the top. Three of the perianth lobes coil back towards the center of the flower head, with many fine and short crinkly hairs and some long straight silky hairs. The [[Stigma (botany)#Style|style]] is 3¾–5½ cm (1½–2¼ in) long, slightly curved towards the center of the flower head, initially yellow but later turning orange. It is topped by a slight thickening that is called the [[pollen presenter]], which is narrow or broadly cone-shaped 1½–4 mm (0.6–1.6 in) long and up to {{convert|2|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide, with the groove that functions as the [[Stigma (botany)|stigma]] central at the very tip. The four scales that subtend the [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] are triangular to awl-shaped and about {{convert|1|mm|in|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=Rourke /><ref name=JSTOR />

== Taxonomy ==
[[Henrik Bernard Oldenland]], the [[Dutch Cape Colony|Cape's]] master gardener of the [[Dutch East India Company]] could have been the first to collect the wart-stemmed pincushion, when he crossed the Outeniqua Mountains near Attaqua's Kloof on an expedition in 1689. The first to describe Oldenland's pincushion was [[Nicolaas Laurens Burman]] in his book ''Florae Capensis Prodromus'', and he named it ''Leucadendron cuneiforme'' in 1768. [[Carl Peter Thunberg]] published a revision of the Proteaceae in 1781, in which he followed [[Carl Linnaeus]] in assigning all species to ''Protea'', and he distinguished ''Protea elliptica''. [[Joseph Knight (horticulturist)|Joseph Knight]] published a book in 1809 titled ''[[On the cultivation of the plants belonging to the natural order of Proteeae]]'', that contained an extensive revision of the [[Proteaceae]] attributed to [[Richard Anthony Salisbury]]. Salisbury moved Thunberg's species to his new genus ''Leucadendrum'', calling it ''Leucadendrum ellipticum''. In addition he recognised two slightly different forms, calling them ''Leucadendrum phyllanthifolium'' and ''Leucadendrum cervinum''. It is assumed that Salisbury had based his review on a draft he had been studying of a paper called ''[[On the natural order of plants called Proteaceae]]'' that [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]] was to publish in 1810. Brown however, called the genus ''Leucospermum'' and made [[Combinatio nova|the new combination]] ''Leucospermum ellipticum'', and further recognised a form he called ''Leucospermum attenuatum''. The French botanist [[Jean Louis Marie Poiret|Jean Poiret]] assigned that last specimen to the genus ''Protea'' in 1816, making the new combination ''P. attenuata''. [[Carl Meissner]] describe a form in 1856, which he named ''Leucospermum zeyheri''. [[Otto Kuntze]] revised the genus in 1891 and called it ''Leucadendron'', a [[homonym]] of a name that had already been used by Linnaeus in 1753 for another group of Proteaceae, which have separate sexes and very large bracts, making the combination ''Leucadendron ellipticum''. [[Michel Gandoger]] finally added ''Leucospermum septemdentatum'' in 1913. In 1932, [[Henry Georges Fourcade]] realised a [[new combination]], ''Leucospermum  phyllanthifolium'', needed to be made for Salisbury's second species. Although the variation in leaf length, leaf toothing and size of the flower heads in ''Leucospermum cuneiforme'' is large, and distant populations may appear to be quite distinct, the characters all change gradually, so it is not possible to determine where subtaxa might start and end. Hence, [[John Patrick Rourke]] in 1970 only recognises one variable species.<ref name=Rourke />

''Leucospermum cuneiforme'' is the [[Type (biology)|type species]] of the cylindric pincushions, [[Section (botany)|section]] ''[[Leucospermum#Crassicaudex|Crassicaudex]]''.

The subtribe Proteinae, to which the genus ''Leucospermum'' has been assigned, consistently has a basic chromosome number of twelve ([[Diploid|2n]]=24).<ref>{{cite journal|first1= L.A.S.|last1= Johnson|first2= Barbara G.|last2= Briggs|year= 1975|title= On the Proteaceae—the evolution and classification of a southern family|journal= Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society|volume= 70|issue= 2|page= 106|doi= 10.1111/j.1095-8339.1975.tb01644.x}}{{dead link|date=April 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

The species name ''cuneiforme'' is compounded from the Latin words ''cuneus'', meaning "wedge" and ''forma'', meaning "form", combined "wedge-shaped".<ref name=SANBI /><ref>{{cite book|first= Richard A.|last= Criley|year= 2010|chapter= 2|title= Leucospermum: Botany and Horticulture|series= Horticultural Reviews|volume= 61|editor= Jules Janick|publisher= John Wiley & Sons|isbn= 978-0-470-65072-1|chapter-url= https://books.google.com/books?id=lVlilno_NacC&pg=PA34}}</ref> The Afrikaans name {{Lang|af|luisiesbos}} "lice bush" comes from the similarity of the seed pods to species of lice.<ref name=JManning>{{cite book | last = Manning | first = John | title = Field Guide to Fynbos | publisher = Struik Publishers | location = Cape Town | page= 270 |  year = 2008 | isbn = 978-1-77007-265-7 }}</ref>

== Distribution, habitat and ecology == 
[[File:Leucospermum cuneiforme Potberg 03.jpg|upright=1.35|thumb|left|Early flowering stage when the pollen presenter is still encased by the perianth claws like a cap]][[File:Leucospermum cuneiforme warts Rebelo.jpg|upright=1.35|thumb|left|The wart-like swellings on older stems are a unique feature of this pincushion species.]]''L. cuneiforme'' has the largest distribution area of the entire genus, and can be found all along the southern coast of the Western Cape and Eastern Cape provinces, and the adjacent mountain ranges between [[Greyton]] (Caledon district) in the west and [[Qolora Mouth]] in Transkei in the east. It occurs in various climatic circumstances with both dominant rain in winter or summer or without a clear-cut peak. The distribution includes [[Riviersonderend Mountains|Riviersonderend]], Potberg, [[Langeberg|Langeberg Range]], [[Outeniqua Mountains|Outeniqua]] and [[Swartberg]] Mountains. It can grow in [[sclerophyll]] [[fynbos]], such as on the south-facing slopes of the Langeberg together with other Proteaceae, ''[[Erica (plant)|Erica]]'' species, ''[[Rutaceae]]'' and ''[[Restionaceae]]'', but also on grassveld, and subtropical dune forests in the Eastern Cape, where it grows together with plants like ''[[Phoenix reclinata]]'' and ''[[Stangeria eriopus]]'', on the arid fringe of the [[Little Karoo]] and the wet margins of the temperate evergreen forests near [[Knysna]] and [[Tsitsikamma National Park|Tsitsikama]]. It does however stick to poor sandy soils derived from [[Table Mountain Sandstone]], [[Witteberg Quartzite]] and stabilised sandy [[Tertiary period|Tertiary]] deposits. It can be found at sea-level as well as up to over {{convert|1000|m|ft|abbr=on}} altitude. ''L. cuneiforme'' is one of the most fire resistant pincushions. Although fire kills the above ground parts of the plant, multiple branches sprout from the rootstock. Mostly, the frequency of the fires makes sure shrubs generally are only ½–1 m (1½–3 ft), but when left unchecked, it develops a dominant stem and grows to about {{convert|3|m|ft|abbr=on}}. Some flowers can be found all year round, but there is a distinct peak from August till February.<ref name=Rourke /> The unscented but conspicuously coloured flower heads are pollinated by birds that feed on the nectar, such as the [[Cape sugarbird]] and some species of sunbird. The birds sit on the flower head and stick their long bills into perianth tubes and so bring their heads and necks in contact with the pollen presenters. Although the flowers are also visited by insects, these do not touch the pollen presenters so do not contribute to the pollination.<ref name=SANBI />

The seeds are covered in a pale fleshy coating called [[elaiosome]] that attracts ants. About two months after flowering, the seeds are ripe and get released from the flower heads, and native ants gather them and carry them to their underground nests. Here, the elaiosome is consumed. The remaining seed is big, slick and hard and the ants cannot remove it. This way the seeds are safe from seed-eaters and fire. This [[seed dispersal syndrome|seed dispersal strategy]] is called [[myrmecochory]]. After a fire, the seeds promptly [[Seed#Inducing germination|germinate]]. So, ''L. cuneiforme'' has two strategies to survive a fire: myrmecochory and resprouting from the rootstock.<ref name=SANBI />

== Cultivation ==
''L. cuneiforme'' is used as an ornamental shrub and is also cultivated as cut flower. There are a few cultivars, such as "Goldie", in addition to several hybrids of ''L. cuneiforme'' with other species.<ref name=SANBI />
